transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-10
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Dr. Nina Rao (CTO - Kepler), Samir Khan (Head of Infra), Lori Menendez (Security PM)

Summary:
Kepler Biotech is evaluating Redwood Private (VPC) for inference workloads that need strict data residency and network isolation. Primary concerns: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, region availability, KMS integration, egress restrictions for air-gapped-ish clusters, and a plan for dedicated capacity vs hosted fallback. They currently run on AWS in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 with a multi-account setup and want a timeline for POC + benchmark.

Topics:
- VPC connectivity options (peering, AWS PrivateLink, Transit Gateway)
- Private endpoints and DNS routing
- IP/CIDR planning and NAT/egress controls
- KMS/HSM and key rotation for model artifacts
- Region constraints and model availability
- Pilot scope and success metrics (latency, throughput, cost)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time, I'm Aisha from Redwood, and we have Marcus, our SE, on the call. Nina, Samir, Lori, thanks for joining. Can you give a quick overview of what you're trying to solve?
[00:12] Nina: Sure, hi. We're Kepler Biotech. We run inference for a bunch of internal tools and some partner-facing models. We're under a couple of compliance constraints, so we want private network, no public endpoints for inference. We're evaluating options — Redwood's private offering looks promising.
[00:28] Samir: To add, we have multi-account AWS, primary region us-east-1, secondary eu-west-1. We want to avoid routing traffic through the public internet. Ideally private endpoints or VPC peering.
[00:38] Marcus: Great, that aligns. We offer Redwood Private with a customer-managed VPC peering option or private endpoints via AWS PrivateLink depending on your topology. Quick Q: do you want bi-directional peering or one-way egress?
[00:49] Lori: One-way egress isn't ideal — we need control on both sides for auditing. Also, how does the KV cache or model artifact sync work over peering?
[01:02] Marcus: Good question. We typically use an S3-backed model store with signed access over the peering link; model artifacts are pulled during deployment. KV cache is in-memory on the GPU nodes, but we do coordinated shard syncing via our control plane. If the control plane is hosted, we can route control plane traffic over PrivateLink.
[01:22] Nina: You said control plane hosted — what are the data flows that still touch Redwood's hosted control plane? Are there inference payloads going to your control plane?
[01:31] Aisha: No inference payloads need to leave your VPC unless you choose hosted inference. For Private VPC the inference plane runs in your network; control plane signals (management, rollouts, metrics streams) can be proxied via PrivateLink. We also offer a private control plane option for enterprise (separate tenancy) if you need full isolation.
[01:52] Samir: OK that helps. What about region constraints — some of our models must stay in eu-west-1 because of partner agreements. Can we run dedicated pools in multiple regions?
[02:03] Marcus: Yes, you can pin dedicated pools per region. We support multi-region model placement. There are model-variant considerations — for example some quantized kernels perform slightly differently between GPU types; we recommend benchmarking in each region.
[02:20] Lori: Security: we need to bring our own KMS. Is HSM integration supported? Key rotation?
[02:27] Marcus: We integrate with customer KMS for encryption at rest for artifacts and config. For HSM-backed keys (CloudHSM / external KMS via BYOK), we can support through our Private deployment installs — we'd need to map the key policies and ensure the compute nodes can access the KMS endpoint over the peering link. Rotation is supported, but we recommend a maintenance window for re-encrypting model artifacts.
[02:47] Nina: Another thing — our egress policy is locked down; only specific endpoints allowed. Will Redwood need outbound internet access from the compute nodes?
[02:55] Aisha: For a fully private topology you can block general outbound internet. We only require connectivity to specific endpoints for metrics/updates unless you host the full control plane. We will provide a network checklist with exact domains/IPs.
[03:07] Samir: Great. On the peering details — we use overlapping CIDRs in some test accounts. Do you support Transit Gateway for shared services rather than direct peering?
[03:16] Marcus: Yes, Transit Gateway works and is common for orgs with shared VPCs. PrivateLink is an alternative if you want to avoid peering and NAT behavior. Each has tradeoffs: peering is simple but requires unique CIDR space; TGW centralizes routing; PrivateLink gives you endpoint network interfaces and more control over egress.
[03:35] Lori: DNS — if we create PrivateLink endpoints, will the model endpoint DNS resolve to the private IPs automatically?
[03:41] Marcus: We'll publish private DNS entries that can be resolved within your VPC. There are some nuances with multi-account shared services; our docs show options for Route 53 private hosted zones and cross-account resolver rules.
[03:56] Nina: What about performance — latency and throughput for LLM inference? We care about p95 latency under 200ms for our simple classification models and throughput of about 200 qps for embedding jobs.
[04:08] Marcus: For the use case you described, we typically recommend a Dedicated pool sized across 3 instances with batching turned on. For embeddings workloads, we can hit your throughput targets with batching and autoscaling. We'll run a benchmark POC to validate.
[04:22] Samir: Can we keep a hosted fallback in case Dedicated nodes fail? Like auto-fail to Redwood hosted but still maintain data controls?
[04:31] Aisha: Yes, we support policy-based routing with fallbacks. If you need to avoid any internet egress at all, then fallback to hosted won't be acceptable. But you can have a hybrid where non-sensitive traffic can fail to hosted.
[04:44] Lori: Compliance check — SOC2, ISO, audit logs. We need to know retention periods, audit log formats.
[04:51] Aisha: We'll send the SOC2 report and an excerpt of our audit log schema. For Private deployments we can ship logs to your S3 or forwarding SIEM over the peering link.
[05:01] Nina: Timeline — we're hoping for a POC in 3-4 weeks. What's realistic?
[05:06] Marcus: If you can provide the CIDRs, IAM roles, and a test account with some sample workloads, we can spin up a pilot in 2-3 weeks. The benchmark run typically takes a few days.
[05:16] Samir: OK I'll share CIDR ranges and the egress policy.
[05:20] Aisha: Perfect. We'll send the network checklist and a draft architecture diagram. Marcus will follow up to schedule the deep dive next Thursday.
[05:29] (cross-talk)
[05:32] Marcus: Quick note — some product names in our docs might show 'Redwood Dedicate' or 'Redwood Private' — apologies for typos in the auto docs, but the features are the same.
[05:44] Nina: No problem. One last question: model updates — how does hot-reload of new model artifacts work without service interruption?
[05:51] Marcus: We stream artifacts to nodes and warm new workers before switching the routing. The KV cache warming is important; for large models we'll recommend canary rollouts.
[06:03] Lori: Sounds good.

Recap & explicit next steps at end of call:
[06:10] Aisha: To recap — Kepler will share CIDRs, sample workloads, and egress rules. Redwood will send security pack (SOC2, audit schema), network checklist, and indicative pricing for a 3-node Dedicated + Private deployment. We'll schedule an architecture deep dive next Thu (Marcus + Samir).
[06:30] Nina: Thanks, talk soon.
